claim: Bacterial persisters within cell cultures constitute a small subpopulation of cells exhibiting a transient antibiotic-tolerant state.
source: Bacterial persisters within cell cultures constitute a small subpopulation of cells exhibiting a transient antibiotic-tolerant state (Balaban et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Balaban et al., 2004

claim: Persisters have traditionally been characterized as non-growing and dormant phenotypes.
source: While persisters have traditionally been characterized as non-growing and dormant phenotypes (Lewis, 2010), recent studies challenge these conventional hallmarks, revealing the heterogeneity of persister cells in terms of growth, metabolism, and other cellular activities (Adams et al., 2011; Arnoldini et al., 2014; Hossain et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2010; Mok et al., 2015b; Orman and Brynildsen, 2013a; Orman and Brynildsen, 2015; Shan et al., 2015; Wakamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lewis, 2010

claim: Recent studies challenge the conventional characterization of persisters as dormant, revealing heterogeneity in growth, metabolism, and cellular activities.
source: While persisters have traditionally been characterized as non-growing and dormant phenotypes (Lewis, 2010), recent studies challenge these conventional hallmarks, revealing the heterogeneity of persister cells in terms of growth, metabolism, and other cellular activities (Adams et al., 2011; Arnoldini et al., 2014; Hossain et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2010; Mok et al., 2015b; Orman and Brynildsen, 2013a; Orman and Brynildsen, 2015; Shan et al., 2015; Wakamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent studies

claim: The transient antibiotic-tolerant state of persister cells promotes recurrent infections.
source: The persistence phenomenon presents a significant health concern (Huemer et al., 2020; Murray et al., 2022), as the transient antibiotic-tolerant state of persister cells promotes recurrent infections (Fisher et al., 2017) and establishes them as a reservoir for the emergence of antibiotic-resistant mutants (Barrett et al., 2019; Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Windels et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fisher et al., 2017

claim: Persister cells establish a reservoir for the emergence of antibiotic-resistant mutants.
source: The persistence phenomenon presents a significant health concern (Huemer et al., 2020; Murray et al., 2022), as the transient antibiotic-tolerant state of persister cells promotes recurrent infections (Fisher et al., 2017) and establishes them as a reservoir for the emergence of antibiotic-resistant mutants (Barrett et al., 2019; Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Windels et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrett et al., 2019; Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Windels et al., 2019

claim: Proliferating tumor cells derive energy predominantly through glycolysis, even in the presence of oxygen, a phenomenon known as aerobic glycolysis.
source: Otto Warburg's research in the early 20th century unveiled an intriguing aspect of mammalian cell metabolism known as 'aerobic glycolysis', wherein proliferating cells (e.g. tumor cells) derive energy predominantly through glycolysis, even in the presence of oxygen (Warburg, 1925).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warburg, 1925

claim: Tumorigenic persisters in a non-proliferating state rely on energy metabolism rather than aerobic glycolysis.
source: Remarkably, tumorigenic persisters that exist in a non-proliferating state may not primarily depend on aerobic glycolysis. Instead, there is substantial evidence suggesting that these cells rely on energy metabolism (Porporato et al., 2018; Vasan et al., 2020); however, the presence of this metabolic state in antibiotic-tolerant bacteria is still a question mark (Orman and Brynildsen, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Porporato et al., 2018; Vasan et al., 2020

claim: The deletion of the cyaA gene resulted in a notable reduction in intracellular cAMP concentration.
source: As anticipated, the deletion of the cyaA gene resulted in a notable reduction in intracellular cAMP concentration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The Δcrp strain exhibited an increase in cAMP concentration, potentially due to the negative feedback regulatory mechanism of the Crp/cAMP complex for the cyaA gene promoter.
source: However, the Δcrp strain exhibited an increase in cAMP concentration, potentially due to the negative feedback regulatory mechanism of the Crp/cAMP complex for the cyaA gene promoter (Keseler et al., 2005; Majerfeld et al., 1981; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citations and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: All three strains (WT, Δcrp, and ΔcyaA) started to enter the stationary phase around 5 hr, with the mutant strains exhibiting slightly lower optical density levels than the WT at this time point.
source: When comparing the growth curves of E. coli wild-type (WT), Δcrp, and ΔcyaA main cultures under identical conditions studied here (see Materials and methods), all three strains started to enter the stationary phase around 5 hr, with the mutant strains exhibiting slightly lower optical density levels than the WT at this time point (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: cAMP levels increase in WT cells during their transition into the stationary phase.
source: Also, our data provide evidence of an increase in cAMP levels in WT cells during their transition into the stationary phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), aligning with existing literature (Bettenbrock et al., 2007; Keseler et al., 2005; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and citations

claim: The WT strain showed a marked increase in both ampicillin- and ofloxacin-persister cells during the late stationary phase, in contrast to the mutant strains, where no such increase was observed.
source: Notably, the WT strain showed a marked increase in both ampicillin- and ofloxacin-persister cells during the late stationary phase, in contrast to the mutant strains, where no such increase was observed (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: The expression of crp restored the persister level in the Δcrp mutant strain.
source: The results demonstrated that the expression of crp restored the persister level in the mutant strain, while the plasmid itself had no impact on persister levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B

claim: After prolonged gentamicin exposure (20 h), the tolerant cell colonies were found to be below the limit of detection for all strains and conditions.
source: After prolonged gentamicin exposure (20 h), the tolerant cell colonies were found to be below the limit of detection for all strains and conditions (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 5C

claim: Deletion of either crp or cyaA in the HipA7 background significantly reduced persistence to both ampicillin and ofloxacin during the late stationary phase.
source: Deletion of either crp or cyaA in the HipA7 background significantly reduced persistence to both ampicillin and ofloxacin during the late stationary phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 8), mirroring the effects observed in the WT strain.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8

claim: Metabolites identified in independent biological replicates of each strain and condition clustered together, confirming the reproducibility of the metabolomics data.
source: The metabolomics data were subjected to unsupervised hierarchical clustering, and metabolites identified in independent biological replicates of each strain and condition were found to cluster together (Figure 2A), thus confirming the reproducibility of our data.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: In the late stationary phase, WT cells maintain their energy metabolism to some extent while downregulating their anabolic pathways.
source: Altogether, our metabolic data indicate that, in the stationary phase, WT cells maintain their energy metabolism to some extent while downregulating their anabolic pathways (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Perturbing the Crp/cAMP complex function leads to a significant downregulation of energy metabolism and an upregulation in the abundance of anabolic metabolites.
source: This metabolic state appears to be regulated by the Crp/cAMP complex, as perturbing its function leads to a significant downregulation of energy metabolism and an upregulation in the abundance of anabolic metabolites (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Proteins identified in independent biological replicates of each strain clustered together in proteomics analysis, confirming the consistency of findings.
source: The resulting proteomics data were subjected to unsupervised hierarchical clustering, and the proteins identified in independent biological replicates of each strain were found to cluster together, confirming the consistency of our findings (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Upregulated pathways in the Δcrp mutant strain are associated with anabolic metabolism and encompass peptidoglycan metabolic processes, cell wall organization or biogenesis, cellular component organization or biogenesis, regulation of cell shape, cell cycle, and cell division.
source: The upregulated pathways are associated with anabolic metabolism and encompass peptidoglycan metabolic processes, cell wall organization or biogenesis, cellular component organization or biogenesis, regulation of cell shape, cell cycle, and cell division (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by proteomics pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The Δcrp mutant strain displayed downregulated pathways, encompassing glycerol metabolism, TCA cycle, pyruvate metabolism, glycolysis, and various pathways associated with ribosome and transcriptional factor activity.
source: Also, the mutant strain displayed downregulated pathways, encompassing glycerol metabolism, TCA cycle, pyruvate metabolism, glycolysis, and various pathways associated with ribosome and transcriptional factor activity (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by proteomics pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: A cluster of proteins involved in energy metabolism and respiratory processes, including GltA, SdhB, SucC, SucD, FrdB, FrdA, AcnA, AceA, and Mdh, were downregulated in the Δcrp mutant strain.
source: Our analysis specifically pinpointed a cluster of proteins involved in energy metabolism and respiratory processes. Notably, this cluster includes GltA, SdhB, SucC, SucD, FrdB, FrdA, AcnA, AceA, and Mdh proteins, which play crucial roles in either the TCA cycle or as membrane-bound components of ETC (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Within the WT strain, a subpopulation from the late stationary phase cultures displayed constant fluorescence levels, indicating their inability to divide.
source: Notably, within the WT strain, a subpopulation from the late stationary phase cultures displayed constant fluorescence levels, indicating their inability to divide (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B

claim: In contrast to the WT strain, similar non-dividing subpopulations were not detected in the mutant strains.
source: In contrast to the WT strain, we did not detect similar subpopulations in the mutant strains (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The growth curve of the WT strain displayed a slower initial growth rate and a prolonged lag phase duration compared to the mutant strains.
source: As anticipated, the growth curve of the WT strain displayed a slower initial growth rate and a prolonged lag phase duration compared to the mutant strains (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry growth curve data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The mutant strains displayed a shorter lag phase, yet they demonstrated an increased doubling time in the exponential phase compared to WT.
source: Conversely, the mutant strains displayed a shorter lag phase, yet they demonstrated an increased doubling time in the exponential phase compared to WT (Figure 4C), which was also anticipated, considering their decreased reliance on oxidative phosphorylation due to TCA cycle inhibition.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry growth curve data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The SQR promoter activity is upregulated in WT cells compared to the mutant strains in the stationary phase.
source: Our results indicate an upregulation of the SQR promoter activity in WT cells compared to the mutant strains in the stationary phase, validating the findings from our metabolomics and proteomics data (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The redox activities of WT cells are much higher and more heterogeneous compared to those of the mutant strains in the late stationary phase.
source: Our data demonstrate that the redox activities of WT cells are much higher and more heterogeneous compared to those of the mutant strains in the late stationary phase, further corroborating the results from our preceding analyses (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by RSG dye assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Tolerant intact cells in WT that survived ampicillin treatment displayed a significant increase in RSG levels compared to cell populations before antibiotic treatments or untreated control cells.
source: While the population-level redox activities of these tolerant intact cells in WT are lower than those of exponential phase cells, they still displayed a significant increase in RSG levels compared to cell populations before antibiotic treatments or untreated control cells subjected to identical conditions (Figure 5D), suggesting that they maintain steady-state energy metabolism.
evidence: Supported by RSG assay data shown in Figure 5D

claim: WT cells exhibit markedly higher VBNC levels than Δcrp and ΔcyaA strains.
source: We want to highlight that not all intact cells in the WT strain reported here are persisters. A significant portion comprises 'viable but non-culturable' (VBNC) cells, and WT cells exhibit markedly higher VBNC levels than Δcrp and ΔcyaA strains (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: Mutant strains associated with the TCA pathway, ETC, ATP synthesis, and mixed acid fermentation pathways exhibited reduced tolerance to both ampicillin and ofloxacin compared to the control E. coli K-12 BW25113 WT strain.
source: However, the mutant strains exhibited reduced tolerance to both antibiotics compared to the control E. coli K-12 BW25113 WT strain, which was found to be largely associated with the TCA pathway (sucA, sucB, lpd, sucC, sucD, sdhA, sdhB, sdhC, sdhD, gltA, acnB, aceE, fumA, mdh and fumC), ETC (nuoB, nuoC, nuoI, nuoK, nuoM, and narV), ATP synthesis (atpA, atpB, atpC, atpD, atpE, and atpH), and mixed acid fermentation pathways (ldhA, fdhF, pta, adhE, and frdC) (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by high-throughput screening data shown in Figure 5E and Supplementary file 4

claim: Knockout strains for key genes associated with the TCA, ETC, and ATP synthase showed reduced antibiotic tolerance, consistent with omics data and screening outcomes.
source: To ensure the reproducibility of our findings, we generated knockout strains for key genes associated with the TCA, ETC, ATP synthase, glycolysis, and pentose phosphate pathway (Figure 5F, see Supplementary file 5 for detailed description of genes). We then tested their antibiotic tolerance, and our results were consistent with the omics data and screening outcomes (Figure 5F), confirming the critical role of energy metabolism, specifically the TCA cycle, ETC, and ATP synthase, in bacterial persistence.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5F

claim: The Crp/cAMP regulatory complex sustains an active respiratory state while downregulating anabolic pathways in persister cells.
source: Through metabolomics, proteomics, and high-throughput screening of single-gene deletion strains, we substantiated that the Crp/cAMP regulatory complex sustains an active respiratory state while downregulating anabolic pathways in persister cells.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics, proteomics, and high-throughput screening data presented in the study

claim: This respiratory state is vital for the survival of persister cells, as perturbing the Crp/cAMP complex or respiration significantly reduced persister phenotypes.
source: This respiratory state is vital for the survival of persister cells, as perturbing the Crp/cAMP complex or respiration significantly reduced persister phenotypes, which may explain the previously reported decrease in antibiotic tolerance in E. coli cells cultured under anaerobic conditions (Orman and Brynildsen, 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Orman and Brynildsen, 2015

claim: An upregulation of anabolic metabolites and proteins associated with cell wall organization, cell cycle, and cell division was observed when the Crp/cAMP regulatory complex was perturbed.
source: Notably, we observed an upregulation of anabolic metabolites and proteins when the Crp/cAMP regulatory complex was perturbed, particularly those associated with cell wall organization, cell cycle, and cell division, enhancing the ability of stationary-phase mutant cells to resume growth.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics and proteomics data

claim: The global metabolic regulator Crp/cAMP redirects the metabolism of antibiotic-tolerant cells from anabolism to oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Our results indicate that the global metabolic regulator Crp/cAMP redirects the metabolism of these antibiotic-tolerant cells from anabolism to oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics and proteomics data presented in the study

claim: Persisters exhibit a reduced metabolic rate compared to rapidly growing exponential-phase cells, but their survival still relies on energy metabolism.
source: Although our data demonstrates that persisters exhibit a reduced metabolic rate compared to rapidly growing exponential-phase cells, their survival still relies on energy metabolism.
evidence: Supported by metabolic assays and knockout screening data

claim: Energy metabolism, specifically the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, electron transport chain (ETC), and ATP synthase, plays a critical role in sustaining persister levels within cell populations.
source: Extensive genomic-level analyses of metabolomics, proteomics, and single-gene deletions consistently highlight the critical role of energy metabolism, specifically the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, electron transport chain (ETC), and ATP synthase, in sustaining persister levels within cell populations.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics, proteomics, and knockout screening data
